Kesari 2 - More than a film it’s a wake up call! 

I was stunned, frozen to my seat from the first frame to the last. My eyes didn’t even flinch once. Kesari 2 didn’t feel like a movie — it felt like a punch to the gut, a scream echoing through history. It was an experience that grips your soul. The intensity, the sacrifice, the sheer will of the characters didn’t let me breathe easy and honestly, it shouldn’t have.

When I got home and heard about the latest terror attacks in Kashmir, my blood was boiling. Are we truly independent? The answer didn’t feel like a yes. If we’re alive today, it’s only because of the unimaginable sacrifices made by those who were slaughtered like animals—without mercy, without justice. Even today, if you visit Jallianwala Bagh you see blood stains on the walls. You can almost hear the cries of babies—2 to 4 months old. It shakes you to your core just to imagine it… and they lived it.

And in the middle of all that darkness, one voice rose. One spark lit up. A 12-year-old boy named Pargat Singh. He opened the eyes of Sankaran Nair. He uncovered the truth of Jallianwala Bagh. And he became a martyr in the process.
More than Sankaran Nair or Dilreet Gill, I want to salute Pargat Singh. Because if it wasn’t for him, we might never have known the real truth behind Jallianwala Bagh. We would’ve continued living in the shadows of the lie that bastard Dyer created.

Kesari 2 doesn’t just tell a story it hits us in the chest. It shakes ours beliefs. It reminds us that our freedom came at a price paid in blood, and that price is still being paid in different ways even today. It’s not just worth watching—it’s necessary. This isn’t just a film. It’s a wake-up call. Watch it—and feel every second of it. It was indeed the BESTEST historical movie I’ve ever watched in my life!

Such utter distortion of history and disgrace to shadow real heroes of independence should be crime. Creating a fictional hero who brought General dyer and Lt. Governor o'dwyer to justice in a trial that never actually happened is so insensitive distortion of history, it shadows the efforts and sentiments of the people of Punjab specifically. The Ghadarites and others. 

The film then flies into some la la land of fantasy. It makes Sankaran Nair team up with a local lawyer to file a case of ‘genocide’ against General Dyer in a local court.

General Dyer was never tried in any court for genocide. In October 1919, the British asked the Hunter Commission to examine some recent ‘disturbances’ in India. The Commission also enquired into the conduct of General Dyer and his claims that he had asked his troops to fire because he feared unrest, anarchy and violence.

Three Indians were part of the Hunter Committee. Sankaran Nair was not one of them. On the basis of the findings of the Committee, General Dyer was relieved of his command in 1920. He died in England, denying all through that he had made a mistake.

Sankaran Nair was a member of the Viceroy’s Executive Council–the precursor to the Indian cabinet–till July 23, 1919. As a member of the council, he agreed to the imposition of Martial Law in Punjab. After his resignation, he joined the then Secretary of State, Edwin Montagu’s council on January 2, 1920

In 1922, many months after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, the findings of the Hunter Commission, and the transfer of Dyer from India, while serving the Indore state as its Diwan, Sankaran Nair wrote a book ‘Gandhi and Anarchy’, a critique of Mahatma Gandhi’s civil disobedience movement. In this book, he “implied the Punjab atrocities were committed with O’Dwyer’s full knowledge and approval.” Michael O’Dwyer was the Lt Governor of Punjab when the massacre took place. General Dyer was the officer who ordered the firing.

O’Dwyer sued Nair for libel and sought an apology. When Nair refused, O’Dwyer took the case to the King’s Bench in London (slightly different from a legal bench).

In the end, Nair lost the case with just one member of the jury favouring him. For his brave fight, Nair was hailed as a hero, and his fight earned him a place in the martyr’s gallery at the Jallianwala Bagh.

The release of Kesari Chapter 2 shows the ongoing exploitation of Sikh history by Bollywood. Jallianwala Bagh, where Sikh families gathered in peace and faced bullets on Vaisakhi, is used here as a background for a story that has little to do with the people who suffered. Sikh lives and voices are treated as material for emotional scenes, while the Sikh spirit that rose from that ground is erased. Bollywood is not engaged in remembrance. It is engaged in extracting whatever it can from Sikh pain to manufacture nationalist entertainment.

Jallianwala Bagh was a direct assault on the Sikh community during one of the holiest days of the Khalsa tradition. The massacre shaped the character of Sikh resistance for the century that followed. In Kesari Chapter 2, this reality is pushed to the side. A Malayali lawyer’s personal awakening is placed at the center while Sikh bodies lie anonymous in the background. There is no trace of the language, spirit, or endurance that defines Sikh history. The massacre is flattened into a generic national tragedy to feed Bollywood’s needs without telling the truth about who stood and who fell.

Bollywood collects Sikh imagery and drapes it over North Indian nationalist fantasy. The casting of Akshay Kumar, who could not even stand with Sikh farmers during a globally historic protest, only underlines the pattern. When Sikh elders sat through the winter fighting for their survival, he chose to side with the government narrative and asked for silence instead of support. Now he returns to use Sikh blood to sell tickets. It is the commercial extraction of another people’s memory for profit.

Sikh suffering does not belong to Bollywood. Sikh blood is not a tool to decorate courtroom dramas and nationalist cinema. Jallianwala Bagh is sacred Sikh ground. Sikhs do not require Bollywood to remember them or misrepresent their history for profit.

Michael O’Dwyer, the Lieutenant-Governor of Punjab during the massacre, was also never tried by the British government.

The only major legal case connected to these figures was when Michael O’Dwyer sued C. Sankaran Nair in the London High Court over statements in Nair’s book “Gandhi and Anarchy”, where Nair held O’Dwyer responsible for the massacre.and Nair lost that case.The irony is that Sankaran Nair was actually a critic of Gandhi, yet the film seems to twist history in a way that aligns with today’s political trend of undermining Gandhi’s legacy.
